The start of the game was delayed for around 10 minutes after the incident.

“We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s game,” UTSA said in a statement. “Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues.”

articles.title: Nueva Ecija farmers raise concerns over land near MTerraSolar project
articles.summary: Farmers in Sitio Sangilo, Gapan City, Nueva Ecija are raising concerns over the MTerra Solar project, saying their livelihood has been affected by road blocks restricting access to their farms.

blocks.text: Farmers in Sitio Sangilo, Gapan City, Nueva Ecija are raising concerns over the MTerra Solar project, saying their livelihood has been affected by road blocks restricting access to their farms.

In a report on "Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho," farmers expressed suspicion that soil has been deliberately dumped along a road to prevent them from reaching their farm land and pressure them into selling it.
However, MTerra Solar Philippines Inc. said the affected area is outside its project site and that it was not responsible for the soil piles.
Blocked road affects livelihood
According to the farmers, the soil dumping began on September 29, with more soil and tree trunks added in the following days.
The road had long served as their route to their farms and as a way to transport their harvest to markets.

One farmer, Marvin, said he could no longer transport his eggplants and chili peppers due to the road block. He estimated that he had spent P60,000 on his crops, some of which were at risk of rotting.
Marvin said the situation had also affected his ability to return to his home, which stands on the land he cultivates. He was temporarily staying with his sibling.
"Malaki pong epekto sa kabuhayanan namin lahat," Marvin said. "Hindi makatao."
["It has a huge impact on all of our livelihoods, it's inhumane."]
The farmers alleged that the soil dumping was meant to force them to sell their land for the solar project. They also questioned why local officials had not acted on their complaints.
Land disputes
Some residents said they had inherited their land from their ancestors and had been cultivating it for years.
The farmers presented approved survey plans and other documents that they said supported their claims to the land.
However, City Assessor Allen Tan said an approved survey plan only shows the shape and boundaries of a property and does not establish ownership.
"Yung titulo po kasi, 'yun lang po ang puwede magpatunay na kayo po ang may-ari ng lupa," Tan said.
["Because the title, that's the only thing that can prove that you are the owner of the land."]
A representative of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said approved plans may be checked against agency records to determine whether titles had already been issued.
The official also explained that people who have possessed public land for at least 20 years may be eligible to apply for a patent title, subject to the applicable requirements.
The land disputes have also led to legal cases.
Lucila said Nueva Ecija 4th District Representative Emerson "Emeng" David Pascual filed three counts of cyber libel against her over videos she posted online.
In a September 2024 Facebook Live statement, Pascual denied taking land from the farmers and said he had checked Gapan'srecords regarding Lucila's claimed property.
"Unang-una, magpapamigay pa ako ng lupa. Pero, hindi ako mang-aagaw ng lupa. Hindi ko po gagawin 'yan kahit kailan," Pascual said.
["First of all, I will even distribute land. But, I am not going to grab land. I will never do that, ever."]
Pascual declined to be interviewed for the KMJS report.
Another farmer, Lito, said he and other residents had faced legal complaints following a confrontation over land surveying and fencing activities. He also expressed concerns for their safety.
Landowner, mayor give their side
Gapan City Mayor Joy Pascual has claimed that the city was not allowing the conversion of land known to still be used for farming.
She also said the disputed area was private property, not a public road, and that the landowner had the documents establishing ownership.
"Ang totoo po niyan, hindi po 'yun sakahan po 'yung lugar po na 'yun, 'yun po ay tinaniman po nila nang wala pong paalam sa may-ari," Pascual said.
["The truth is, that place isn't a farm, they just planted on it without permission from the owner."]
The mayor said residents who could establish that they had permission to cultivate the land could approach City Hall so their claims could be checked.
Businessman and landowner Engineer Renato Tan also denied that the disputed property belonged to the farmers.
"Meron po talaga 'yan. Kaya binili po namin 'yan na puro may titulo. Hindi po sa kanila. Sila po mga sumasakay lang po sa mga lupa roon. Wala po silang mga pag-aari," he said.
["They really have (titles). That's why we bought that [land] where everything has a title. It doesn't belong to them. They are just squatting on the lands there. They don't own anything.]
Tan said he had the right to manage his property and that the residents could use another route.

Barangay Captain Benigno said he had issued summons to the parties involved to discuss the dispute but that they had not appeared as expected. He urged the residents to meet with barangay officials so they could present their claims and discuss a possible resolution.
MTerra Solar says disputed area is outside project
MTerra Solar is being developed by Terra Solar Philippines Inc., which is backed by Meralco PowerGen Corp. and US-based investment firm Actis.

The project covers about 4,500 hectares across four towns in Nueva Ecija and one town in Bulacan. Its developers aim to make it the world's largest solar and battery energy storage facility when completed.
Construction began in November 2024, while Phase 1 was inaugurated in July 2026. The project is expected to be completed next year.
Company representatives said the facility is intended to help supply electricity to about 2.5 million households. Its battery storage system will also allow excess solar power to be used at night.
When asked about the farmers' complaints, Atty. Christer A. Gaudiano, MGEN Sustainability, Communications and External Affairs Head said the affected area was not part of the project.

"Unfortunately 'yung area na 'yun ay outside the project scope ng Terra Solar. 'Yung access nila, hindi po sa amin 'yun, hindi rin po kami 'yung naglagay po ng mga tambak na 'yun at medyo malayo rin po 'yun dito sa project site," he said.
["Unfortunately, that area is outside the project scope of Terra Solar. Their access is not ours, we also didn't place those piles of land and it's also quite far from the project site here."]

The company also said most of the land within its project site had previously been idle or used for poultry and livestock raising. It is working with Central Luzon State University on an agrivoltaic study to explore growing crops and vegetables beneath solar panels.

Company representatives said they hold monthly consultations with communities in affected areas and have provided at least P100 million worth of community projects over the past two years, including solar streetlights, water systems, a fire truck, and training for potential workers.
Experts, groups discuss agriculture and renewable energy

The Department of Agriculture acknowledged the importance of farming to Nueva Ecija, one of the country's major crop-producing provinces. It said renewable energy projects should take agricultural land and farmers' livelihoods into account.

"Hindi naman po ibig sabihin na ang paggamit natin ng solar energy ay makakaapekto sa ating agrikultura. 'Yun nga lang po, sana sa paglalagay po natin o sa pag-set up ng mga solar farms ay kino-consider din po natin 'yung ating mga agricultural land para hindi maapektuhan ang ating production at hindi maapektuhan ang kabuhayan ng ating mga magsasaka," Department of Agriculture Region 3 Field Operations Division Acting Chief Lowell Rebillaco said.

["It doesn't mean that our use of solar energy will negatively affect our agriculture. It's just that, hopefully, in placing or setting up these solar farms, we also consider our agricultural lands so that our production and the livelihood of our farmers won't be affected."]
The Energy Regulatory Commission, meanwhile, said solar power is a clean and sustainable energy source that can help provide a stable electricity supply and lower power costs.
Farmers' groups and advocates also raised concerns about the effects of large solar projects on agricultural land and rural communities.
A representative of MADSOLAR said the group does not oppose renewable energy but is concerned about projects that could damage farmland and affect farmers' livelihoods.
The Unyon ng mga Manggagawa sa Agrikultura (UMA) also called for stronger government support for farmers, including subsidies and assistance for agricultural production.

Meanwhile, Makabayan bloc Representative Renee Co raised concerns about possible soil degradation, erosion, and other environmental effects of large solar farms, saying these concerns should be supported by sufficient data. —JCB, GMA News

articles.title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
articles.summary: An expedition to a remote Pacific island hoping to uncover the American aviator's wreckage was on hold for three days.

blocks.text: Image source, Purdue University
Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited"
A search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.

A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.
The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.
Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday.
"We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.
The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest.

But the weather - powered by strong El Niño conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937
"We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited."
Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.
From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.
But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.
One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro

blocks.text: Image source, Archaeological Legacy Institute
A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro
Interest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish, external previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday.

While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11.
Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island.
To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.
But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Images from 1938 released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand this week show Nikumaroro - then Gardner Island - with the SS Norwich City wreck in the bottom right corner

blocks.text: Image source, RNZAF
Images from 1938 released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand this week show Nikumaroro - then Gardner Island - with the SS Norwich City wreck in the bottom right corner
However, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory.

Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City.

As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane.

ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days.

blocks.caption: Map showing the relative locations of Papua New Guinea, Hawaii, Australia, Howland Island and Kikumaroro Island

blocks.text: While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon.
Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.

In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.
Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

blocks.caption: A satellite image of Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean showing the location of the Taraia Object

articles.title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
articles.summary: Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left…

image.caption: Glucksmann has a difficult campaign ahead as the Socialist candidateImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).
The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

blocks.caption: Glucksmann was flour-bombed while leaving his victory celebrationImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gluckmann's rapid rise

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.
France students demand better schools
Melenchon's youth appeal

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

blocks.caption: Melenchon in Paris during a public sector strike on September 29Image: Tom Nicholson/REUTERS

blocks.text: Glucksmann's youth efforts

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Forget the seven-year itch: opposite-sex marriages more likely to end after two decades
articles.summary:
ONS data for England and Wales shows 26% of heterosexual divorces in 2025 followed 20 years or more of marriage

Most couples are aware of the dreaded “seven-year itch”, when the honeymoon…

blocks.text: Most couples are aware of the dreaded “seven-year itch”, when the honeymoon period wears off and real life starts to bite.

Now official data has shown that couples in England and Wales are more likely to split after 20 years. According to Office for National Statistics figures, more than a quarter of all divorces between opposite-sex couples happened after 20 years or longer of marriage.

Some celebrities have recently displayed the “20-year itch”, with the former Strictly presenter Tess Daly separating from her husband, Vernon Kay, after 22 years of marriage. The Downton Abbey actor Hugh Bonneville split from his wife, Lulu Williams, in 2023 after 25 years, and in 2019, Colin Firth announced his separation from wife, Livia Giuggioli, after 22. Last year, the Hollywood star Nicole Kidman and and singer Keith Urban separated after almost 20 years of marriage.

Divorce lawyers have previously said some couples are putting off splitting up because of the cost of living crisis. Recent figures have shown the average length of a marriage ending in divorce in England and Wales reached a record high last year.

ONS figures have long shown that the seven-year itch appears to exist; since records began in 1963, the largest proportion of divorces each year has almost always been among those who have spent between five to nine years as a couple.

Just over a quarter (26%) of the 102,879 divorces involving opposite-sex couples in England and Wales last year had been married for 20 years or more, while 23% were between five and nine years. This is the second time the five- to nine-year category has been pushed to second place. In the mid-1980s it happened when a new law cut the minimum term of a marriage from three years to one.

Divorce lawyers think the rise of the divorce after 20 years is due to couples staying together for the sake of the children. Lisa Pepper, a divorce lawyer at Osbornes Law, told the Sunday Times: “The largest percentage of cases I see are after a long marriage. Staying together for the sake of the children is true.”

The trend is also happening in the US: a Pew research group study found the incidents of those divorcing after 20 years had doubled since the 1990s. Researchers cautioned: “Divorce at this stage of life can also have some downsides. Grey divorcees tend to be less financially secure than married and widowed adults, particularly among women. And living alone at older ages can be detrimental to one’s financial comfort and, for men, their satisfaction with their social lives.”

Analysis from the US law firm Weinberger found: “Marrying for life is no longer seen as the pinnacle of successful adulthood – especially in more progressive areas of the country. Those who have adequate financial resources to flourish solo may feel more freedom to uncouple.
“With less societal pressure to stay together no matter what, ‘grey divorcees’ have more ‘permission’ to unshackle themselves from unhappy marriages and make the best of their golden years.”

Earlier ONS figures for England and Wales found the average marriage ending in divorce in 2025 lasted for 13 years. This is the longest since records began in 1963 and up from a record low of 8.9 years in 1985.
Rebecca Aston‑Jones, a senior associate at Clarke Willmott, a law firm that specialises in divorce, said the rising cost of living was keeping unhappy couples together.
“One of the main factors discouraging people from pursuing a divorce is the significant financial pressure that comes with establishing and maintaining two separate households,” she said.

articles.title: PCG drives away foreign fishing vessel from Kota Island
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove away an unauthorized foreign fishing vessel from the territorial sea of Kota Island in the West Philippine Sea on Sunday, Oct.…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) drove away an unauthorized foreign fishing vessel from the territorial sea of Kota Island in the West Philippine Sea on Sunday, Oct. 18, in its fourth such operation in three weeks, according to PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela.

The PCG said its High-Speed Response Boat (HSRB-019), while en route to Kota Island, spotted the vessel about 1.75 nautical miles north-northwest of the island, within the Philippines’ 12-nautical-mile territorial sea.
HSRB-019 immediately reinforced two PCG rubber boats already engaging the vessel. The three boats maintained a close presence and repeatedly ordered the foreign vessel by radio to leave the area.
The vessel eventually withdrew without reported incidents, the PCG said.
The latest operation followed three earlier incidents involving foreign vessels near Kota Island on Sept. 28, Oct. 9 and Oct. 11.
On Sept. 28 and Oct. 9, the PCG drove away Chinese maritime militia vessel 9622 and its accompanying small boats, while five foreign fishing vessels were driven away on Oct. 11.
On Oct. 15, the PCG also drove away a Chinese fishing vessel and four small boats from the waters of Lawak Island.
Kota Island is part of the Municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan and lies within the Kalayaan Island Group.

The PCG said foreign vessels are prohibited from fishing in the Philippines’ territorial sea without authorization, citing international law, the Philippine Fisheries Code and the Philippine Maritime Zones Act.
Under PCG Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan, the agency said it would sustain its maritime patrols in the Kalayaan Island Group in coordination with the Philippine Marine Corps.
The deployment of HSRB-019 is intended to strengthen the Coast Guard’s ability to respond swiftly to maritime intrusions, it added.

The operation was conducted in line with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to uphold the Philippines’ rights under the 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea and protect the country’s maritime territory and Filipino fishermen, the PCG said. /das

articles.title: Microsoft drops huge AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns
articles.summary:
Development by UK firm Nscale heralded by ministers as largest of its kind in the country loses its anchor tenant

The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has…

blocks.text: The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies.
The development by the British company Nscale, heralded by ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, was planned to open at Loughton in Essex next year.
Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the location was still an operational scaffolding yard.
Now there are further concerns after Microsoft, one of its largest planned customers and expected to have been the anchor tenant, informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement.
It comes a month after it emerged that power supply problems meant the project would face a lengthy wait before coming online.

Keir Starmer’s government had highlighted the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing it as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.

The end of the deal with Microsoft, first reported in the Telegraph, means Nscale has lost its only publicly announced customer for the Essex datacentre. It is understood that Microsoft remains on board for another project the company has in Norway.

Nscale, which is backed by tech companies including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre provider but the loss of an anchor tenant for its Loughton project could undermine its ambition to float on Wall Street this year with a potential valuation of $35bn (£26bn).
An Nscale spokesperson said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.
“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

articles.title: EPA quietly backtracks on claims US has phased out toxic Pfas compounds
articles.summary:
Agency changes wording on website as Texas-based chemical firm continues manufacture of plastic containers

The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US…

blocks.text: The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly backtracked on a claim that the US has phased out two of the most dangerous Pfas compounds – Pfoa and Pfos.

The EPA has found that virtually no level of exposure to either in drinking water is safe, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies Pfoa as “carcinogenic to humans” and Pfos as “possibly carcinogenic”. Still, the EPA is allowing Houston-based Inhance to produce containers from which Pfoa has been found to leach at high levels into the containers’ contents. The company makes up to 200m plastic containers annually used across the US economy.

The containers present an “ongoing serious and ongoing threat to public health,” said Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist who is now science policy director with the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (Peer) non-profit.
Inhance has denied that the chemical leaches out in measurable levels, and told The Guardian in a statement that any Pfoa from its products are an “impurity”

The “phase-out” was put in place after documents made public during landmark early 2000s litigation on DuPont’s Pfas pollution in West Virginia laid bare the ubiquitous chemicals’ dangers and serious health risks. In 2015, facing intense pressure to act, the EPA reached an agreement with eight Pfas producers to “phase out” production of Pfoa and Pfos, a similar chemical produced by 3M.

Though the agency stopped short of a ban, the “phase out” was viewed as major progress on reining in Pfas pollution. Officials often repeated the claim that the chemicals had been phased out, giving the impression that they were no longer produced or used in the US.

Last month, the EPA quietly changed wording on its website that claimed Pfoa and Pfos had been phased out.. In fact, both have been produced in the US this whole time, and at levels that independent science suggest are quite high.
The EPA site previously stated: “The manufacture and import of Pfoa has also been phased out in the United States.”
It now reads: “Quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported, and used by companies … ”

The change was made in response to a complaint filed by Peer, which pointed out that the EPA was allowing Pfoa to be produced in the US. Under the Information Quality Act, data and information made public by federal agencies be complete and accurate.

“They were giving the false impression and saying, ‘Nothing to see here because Pfoa is not being produced in the US,’” Bennett told the Guardian. “But that was demonstrably false, and now they have admitted it.”

An epidemiological panel convened during the West Virginia DuPont case found Pfoa and Pfos likely causes cancer, heart disease, liver disease, kidney disease. The panel’s findings were the scientific basis for the phase-out.

The EPA did not immediately provide a comment to the Guardian. Inhance in its statement to The Guardian stressed that there was never a ban in place and it was not one of the eight companies that agreed to stop producing Pfoa.
The reversal underscores why phase-outs are inadequate, and the EPA needs to put in place bans, Bennett said.

“If you have a chemical and there’s no safe level of it, then why on earth would you allow it to be manufactured?” she said. “This all makes perfect sense if you understand the reality that the EPA is an arm of industry, especially under the Trump administration.”
The EPA’s reversal marks the latest twist in a six-year legal battle over Inhance’s Pfoa-infused containers.

The EPA seemed unaware that Pfas were being added to plastic containers until late 2020 testing by Peer found high levels of Pfas in pesticides stored in Inhance bins. The subsequent EPA investigation unearthed wide-scale contamination of plastic containers, prompting the agency to subpoena Inhance for information.

It publicly reminded the plastics industry that companies must submit for a safety review if they manufacture Pfoa. Inhance dismissed the agency’s evidence and claimed its containers did not leech Pfoa, but the EPA disagreed, again ordering Inhance in March 2022 to “immediately cease” production.
Two weeks later, Inhance put out a press release stating that its products did not “impart” Pfoa, and it did not cease production.

Subsequent EPA testing found the containers still contained Pfoa. Facing legal pressure from Peer, the EPA by December 2023 again ordered Inhance to stop making the containers. That ban was overturned by a federal appeals court. Peer later sued, but the case was dismissed because a federal judge ruled that the group lacked standing.
In its statement, Inhance said that it made adjustments to reduce by 90% the level of Pfoa “impurities”.

“Published peer-reviewed third-party risk assessments conclude that estimated exposure does not present an unreasonable risk to human health or the environment,” Inhance chief operating officer Patricia van Ee wrote. “We have shared our process data with EPA throughout its review.”

The EPA appears to have given up on enforcing the phase out and legally pressuring Inhance. Still, the EPA maintained on its website that Pfoa had been phased out of production, drawing the formal complaint from Peer.
In a response dated 18 September, EPA assistant administrator for chemical safety and pollution prevention, Douglas Troutman, wrote: “In response to Peer’s request, the EPA is updating its websites.”
The update also notes that Pfos is in US production in some “limited, ongoing uses”.

“This rare touch of candor by EPA is welcome, but it does not address the free flow of toxic Pfas saturating our food, water, and soil,” Bennett said. “Now that EPA has admitted that these two legacy Pfas are still manufactured in the US, it is past time to take effective enforcement action.”

articles.title: Some conservative states aren’t using Medicaid hardship exemption – for political reasons
articles.summary:
States like Missouri and Iowa are choosing to not take up exemption designed to help low-income people keep coverage during hardship

Some conservative states that have rejected hardship…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: Some conservative states that have rejected hardship exemptions for the new Medicaid requirements may be choosing not to due to political reasons, experts say.

New federal work requirements for Medicaid, slated to come into effect on 1 January, mean that adults enrolled through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid expansion will have to work, attend school, volunteer, or take part in another qualifying activity at least 80 hours a month to maintain their coverage.

The bill also includes federal exemptions designed to help low-income people keep their Medicaid coverage when they are hospitalized, have to travel for medical care, or if they live in areas affected by disasters or high unemployment.
Most recently, New York City has adopted the high-unemployment exemption for the Bronx, where about 200,000 residents would otherwise have been subject to the new requirements.

However, some states like Missouri and Iowa are choosing not to take up this exemption for its residents, per new research by the healthcare policy nonprofit KFF, despite having counties that would qualify for this exemption.
The Guardian has contacted both the Missouri and Iowa state departments for comment.
Experts have noted to the Guardian why this could be the case – including states not wanting the extra administrative burden and varying political factors.
Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured, pointed to ideological opposition.

“If [state officials] are advocates of work requirements, they may feel like these work requirements should apply to everyone evenly and whether someone lives in a county with high unemployment or not really shouldn’t be a factor,” Tolbert said.

“It could also be an administrative burden, too, if the state were to adopt this hardship exception they have to submit the data on an ongoing basis to CMS and then they have to make sure their system, their eligibility system is able to blanket exempt or exclude people from these work requirements based on where they live and they’re living in a particular county. So that could be a factor as well.”
Sarah H Gordon, associate professor at the Boston University School of Public Health, also pointed to politics coming into play behind these states’ decisions.

“States that are not taking up the hardship exemption tend to be more politically conservative states that typically align with the idea that health insurance should be tied to employment or other community engagement activities,” Gordon said. “Medicaid is a federal program and there is a lot of variation between states.”

She added: “Not taking up that exemption is partly political. We have states that are taking up work requirements early, states that are taking less time to make sure they understand the new requirements. This is just a patchwork of implementation where some states are going above and beyond to try and minimize coverage losses and other states really aren’t and way more people will lose coverage.”

Joel Ferber, director of advocacy at Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, said that it was “disappointing” that the state was not currently planing to take up these exemptions that could potentially benefit its residents.
“They say that they are not because they don’t want to create additional bureaucratic burdens of its participants, but this doesn’t make sense.

“If you polled Medicaid participants and said to them, would you rather lose your healthcare or fill out a hardship form, 100% of them would likely choose to fill out the form. So it just doesn’t make sense,” he continued.

Most notably, the introduction of these new requirements will result in millions of Americans losing their healthcare coverage. A clear example of this policy in action is in Arkansas, which introduced Medicaid work requirements in 2018. By the end of that year, more than 18,000 people had lost coverage, yet researchers found no significant increase in employment.
Jacob Wallace, associate professor at the Yale School of Public Health and an expert on Medicaid, called the new work requirements “very concerning”.

“Historically, they don’t encourage people to work, but they do seem to generate administrative burdens and paperwork that leads to people dropping off the program,” Wallace said. “There’s a very broad concern about the loss of coverage that is likely to happen, and hopefully states are trying to mitigate those losses as best as they can.”

He added: “And the more hoops we ask people to jump through to exempt themselves or qualify themselves for work requirements, the more people we lose just because we don’t have the right address, or phone number. We send the paperwork but it’s confusing and we don’t provide enough support for people to do the paperwork.”

AI photos are making it harder to know what you're booking on Airbnb. Here's what to look out for

When booking his trip to Montreal, Wells found extremely polished-looking photos of hosts appeared in numerous Airbnb listings, leading him to suspect they had been generated using AI. Short-term rentals in that city are subject to strict rules aimed in part at protecting the city's housing supply. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

Josh Wells, a college student from Iowa, was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through Airbnb listings in search of a place to stay, he began to notice something that didn't seem quite right.
Several of the hosts renting out their properties had profile pictures that Wells suspected were generated by artificial intelligence.
"Your average person taking an iPhone photo, there's obviously like a little bit of imperfections," Wells told the CBC's Cost of Living. "The AI photos, they just looked too perfect."
Still, Wells kept browsing. He was even close to booking one of the properties when a final look at the listing's photos raised another red flag.

He zoomed in on a piece of wall art depicting two halves of faces joined together. At the top, the artwork appeared to read "Picasso." But in another photo of the same room, taken from a different angle, the artwork looked different.
"The text was all warped and funky," he said. "I'm just like, 'Yeah, OK, this is AI."

That was enough to put Wells off the listing — and ultimately using Airbnb for this trip. Unable to tell whether the photos showed a real place or an AI-generated version, he opted for an apartment-style hotel instead.
"The fake profile picture is one thing, but listings of the actual place that you're staying at and spending thousands of dollars was an immediate no for me.”
Wells isn't the only traveller to question whether the photos found on Airbnb or similar short-term rental-style platforms accurately reflect reality.

As AI makes it easier to alter photos, experts say travellers may find it increasingly difficult to know whether Airbnb-style listings accurately reflect reality, raising questions about consumer trust and protections in Canada.

In a statement to CBC News, Airbnb said its rules require listings to be "accurately represented" and that the company may ask hosts to remove content that uses AI or other digital technology to "edit flaws, hide damage, add amenities or attributes that are not part of a listing, or otherwise materially misrepresent the listing."

The company further said it encourages guests to report misleading listings and that those who find a property that doesn't match its description can contact its 24/7 community support team. Under AirCover, Airbnb added, it may help guests find a similar place or provide a refund if the host can't resolve the issue.
We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains
Ultra-processed foods could damage your brain: study
Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know isn't the healthiest choice.

A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.

But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.
Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health, and could even be linked to some types of cancer.

But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University, published Thursday by JAMA Network Open, signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.

The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.
People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.
But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.

articles.title: Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
articles.summary: At least one person was killed in the strikes, which also hit a data centre used by Russia's equivalent of Facebook.

blocks.text: At least one person has been killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that successfully targeted two of the city's oil facilities.
The region's Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being extinguished at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot following the attack, which also injured at least five.
A logistics centre belonging to Ozon - known as Russia's Amazon - and a data centre belonging to Facebook equivalent VKontakte were also hit.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strikes. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday morning that Russia had targeted his country's energy sector 76 times since Donald Trump declared an "energy ceasefire" last week.

Ukraine had paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities - which it says are to limit the main revenue stream for Moscow's war effort - for three days after the announcement, while accusing Russia of continuing.
It then resumed strikes earlier this week, drawing the ire of Trump, who called for a truce to facilitate a deal he struck with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.
Ukraine has struck St Petersburg before, though regions closer to Ukraine are threatened more often. The city's oil terminal was last hit in July.
Russia's defence ministry said it had shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday.
St Petersburg's governor said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged in the attacks on the city, while Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.
He also said mobile internet service disruption was possible.
Social network VK confirmed a drone had targeted its regional data centre, but stressed its services were available "as usual" after users reported outages in the early hours of the morning.
Ozon also confirmed its local logistics centre had been targeted by a drone, sparking a fire.
It said staff were evacuated and no one was injured, and that it was not accepting shipments from sellers at the location "as it is currently serving other operational purposes".

As well as numerous oil facilities across Russia, Ukraine has also mounted strikes aimed at disrupting the Russian economy more broadly. Earlier this month, it launched a series of attacks on Yandex, Russia's largest search engine, that led to service disruptions.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have frayed since the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war, ahead of the midterm elections.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
Trump's decision to temporarily suspend a raft of sanctions against Russia has brought fresh criticism, including from some US Republicans.
Both Russia and Ukraine have been striking one another's energy infrastructure with increasing intensity ahead of the winter, as Moscow's full-scale invasion drags on in its fifth year.
Russia says it hits targets used by Ukraine's military, though the UN noted on Friday that the first two weeks of October had been the deadliest for Ukrainian civilians in years.
Russian strikes on energy facilities have left hundreds of thousands without power, raising concerns about civilians enduring another freezing winter.

Zelensky said on Saturday that tens of thousands of people were still without power. Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, most of which were aimed at energy facilities, he said.

articles.title: ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
articles.summary:
Hundreds at Lisbon tent camp demand action on housing, as Giorgia Meloni says march in Italian capital exploited by ‘hooligans’

The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in…
articles.byline: Sam Jones in Madrid and agencies

blocks.text: The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal, with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.

A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.

blocks.caption: Riot police and protesters clashing in Milan. Photograph: Stringer/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”.
In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – following a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.

blocks.caption: The tent camp in Rossio Square. Photograph: Manuel Fuentes/EPA

blocks.text: The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square.

“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.”

Antonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.

Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Lisbon Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up.
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.

Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understands that people want to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France.
after newsletter promotion

There have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week, where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama.

blocks.caption: A car on fire during an anti-government demonstration outside the prime minister's office in Tirana on Saturday. Photograph: Hameraldi Agolli/AP

blocks.text: On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.

In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump.

Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat.

The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.

In France, fury over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

image.caption: A car burns after a Russian airstrike on a residential neighbourhood in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Kateryna Klochko/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
Ukraine targets Russian oil sites, while Russia launches attacks on Zaporizhzhia
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data centre for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.

items: Zelenskyy urges support for new U.S. sanctions on Russia hours after Trump paused them

blocks.text: Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a six-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia Saturday, local officials said.
A local man carries carries buckets of broken glass in front a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Kateryna Klochko/The Associated Press)
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.

articles.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
articles.summary: Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection…

image.caption: Leuna, in Saxony-Anhalt, has become one of Germany's major hubs for the chemical industry and oil refineriesImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.
Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits
Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."
4-day workweek: A model for the future?
CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.
A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."
SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.
An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

blocks.caption: Bärbel Bas' reform plan had the CDU up in armsImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.
Why the reform stalled
At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: France reports more than 1,800 arrests after riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests
articles.summary: Rioters torched public buildings and looted shops across France, destroying Limoges' historic town hall. The violence erupted during nationwide cost-of-living protests.

image.caption: Clashes also broke out in Marseille before a demonstration against high living costsImage: Thibaud Moritz/AFP

blocks.text: More than 1,800 people were arrested across France following riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday.
The unrest on Saturday has sharpened tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, as anger over living costs collides with tight limits on government spending.
France protests turn violent nationwide
What happened during the protests?

Clashes, fires and looting broke out in several cities during Saturday's demonstrations. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 150 police officers had been injured and blamed what he described as a highly organized, violent far-left group.

Paris police reported 855 arrests, describing the figure as a record. Prosecutors said 517 people remained in custody, including 171 minors. Those figures were provisional, with arrests continuing until early Sunday.
Most arrests in the capital were linked to suspected handling of stolen goods, participation in a group intending to commit violence, and vandalism.
In central France, rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall, leaving much of it gutted. Mayor Guillaume Guerin condemned the destruction.
"There are no words to condemn what happened, so appalling is it," he told broadcaster LCI. "The country is in chaos."

blocks.caption: Rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall during nationwide demonstrations over living costsImage: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP

blocks.text: Authorities reported attacks on public buildings and shops in Marseille, Lyon, Avignon and Grenoble. Police used tear gas, batons and water cannon in several cities.
Demonstrators were also reported injured. The newspaper Le Figaro reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand to a grenade fired by police in Saint-Étienne.
What have leading French politicians said?
President Emmanuel Macron vowed that those responsible would be prosecuted and punished.
"No room for violence in our Republic," he wrote on X, condemning attacks on government buildings, businesses and town halls.
Opposition politicians seeking to succeed Macron in presidential elections in April and May also responded to the unrest.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen accused the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon of having "legitimized the violence." She pledged to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."
France protests escalate as unrest spreads across cities
Melenchon, who had backed the demonstrations and preceding student protests, urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."

The demonstrations brought together grievances over fuel prices, low wages and problems facing farmers and firefighters. School and university students demanding better learning conditions also participated.
The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union gave a higher national estimate of 800,000.
France's high debt and budget deficit limit the government's ability to meet demands for additional spending.
Online calls to revive the yellow vest movement have added to government concerns that student demonstrations could grow into broader unrest.

The yellow vest movement began in 2018 over planned fuel tax increases and grew into wider protests over living costs and inequality. Named after the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, it brought months of nationwide demonstrations, some marked by violent clashes with police.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] China’s envoy: Sounds like a threat, walks like a threat
articles.summary: The reality on the ground and at sea is that a 'peace-loving' China can still inflict harm — economically and physically

blocks.text: Since 2026, the Chinese embassy in Manila has made it normal to issue strong, sometimes incendiary, statements against Philippine agencies and officials, including the nationally-elected kind. It’s language that has teetered close to gutter-level, particularly when it’s the exchanges between its deputy spokesperson Guo Wei and Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, who speaks for the Philippine Coast Guard on the West Philippine Sea.

Yet it was still quite surprising — even if it was arguably expected — for Beijing’s top diplomat in the Philippines, Ambassador Jing Quan, to say the Philippines “should feel fortunate” that China doesn’t use force in its maritime disputes. If it did, the veteran diplomat said, “we may easily win.”
“But no, we will not choose to use force. We love peace,” he told reporters on October 15, on the sidelines of a forum.

Jing went on to mention regions in the world — Gaza and Venezuela — where conflicts launched by Israel and the United States, respectively, have triggered instability in the region. The ambassador conveniently left out two other major conflicts in the world: the Israel and US war on Iran, and Russia’s war on Ukraine.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), in a rare strongly-worded but terse statement, chastised Jing for his remarks.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is expected to summon the Chinese envoy for the second time in less than a year over the same remarks, which he characterized as a “threat.”

The Chinese embassy has pushed back against the DFA through a statement and against Marcos through a vaguely-worded tweet (“Is this a threat?” to caption a longer clip of the chance interview with the media).
In the five-minute interview, Jing goes on about the importance of dialogue in Asia, including within Southeast Asia, which is negotiating a South China Sea code with China.

But the minutes preceding and succeeding that one line about the use of force doesn’t really take away from how out-of-pocket it was — to insist that Manila should be grateful that its superpower neighbor “loves” peace because, if it did not, it would handily win.

Because the reality on the ground and at sea is that a “peace-loving” China can still inflict harm — economically and physically. Filipino personnel have been injured, to varying degrees, from the water cannons the China Coast Guard (CCG) uses to drive away maritime missions to key features in the West Philippine Sea.

Literal blood has been shed by soldiers inadvertently injured during confrontations — a finger was severed in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in June 2024, and one soldier sustained a head injury just in July 2026. Earlier in October, the medical evacuation of a soldier with appendicitis took 10 hours because the CCG insisted on their way of doing things during the mission.
Fisherfolk in Zambales, Palawan, and other fishing communities that have historically relied on the West Philippine Sea speak of dwindling catches or the lack of any opportunity to fish at all.

During embeds in Navy warships on West Philippine Sea missions, I’ve come to almost expect the presence of a Chinese navy warship. I have to actively remind myself that while this has become the norm, it should not be accepted as such.
Such is the “reset” that Marcos signalled and Filipino diplomats have aspired for since the beginning of 2026.

The information ecosystem when it comes to discussions on the West Philippine Sea and the disputes between the Philippines and China is, no doubt, full of noise — many of it the manufactured kind that’s designed to obfuscate from the facts on hand.

Information and influence operations want to wear down the Filipino soldier and civilian’s spirit to wanting to defend what is the Filipinos’ by spotlighting Chinese narratives: that resistance is futile, or that it’s a binary choice between war and peace.

I sometimes find myself having to discern whether a statement from either the embassy or a Philippine government official ought to be highlighted and amplified. He-said-he-said and tits-for-tats are easy and fun to draw out, sure. But they don’t always help readers make sense of what’s going on between the two countries in terms of maritime, political, or diplomatic issues.

Recently, journalism students interviewed me for a school project. At one point, they asked me: How do you sift through the noise in diplomacy when, in some cases, either side has their own truth that they want amplified?

The answer can be simple, I told them. You go back to what international law, including the 2016 Arbitral Award, says. In reconstructing events that are not available for the public or even journalists to see, you talk to the widest range of sources, including those who could be adversarial to your personal beliefs.
You probe, you ask — and then you second-guess yourself. Rinse, repeat.
In conversations with sources, there have been worries that, in all the noise, advocates and experts — even the most earnest ones — are in danger of losing the plot.

The burden then falls onto the bureaucrats, the credentialed experts, and journalists who’ve done their homework to sift through propaganda, spin, and political noise, and stay laser-focused on key truths: that Manila must defend its entitlements and claims in the West Philippine Sea while also trying to keep okay ties with a sometimes-renegade Beijing.

For the military, that means keeping vigilant, especially with the 2028 presidential elections forthcoming, while still keeping itself free of partisan and electoral politicking. It means amping up its external defense posture, which, 15 years since the revised AFP modernization act, means focusing on logistics and supply chains. What good are new and shiny military toys when there’s little space to service them?

We recently published a two-part report on the military’s modernization and defense self-reliance efforts. Because as we keep close track of both escalating rhetoric and confrontations in the West Philippine Sea, it’s important to keep an eye on how the Philippines’ maritime frontliners are preparing for any and all eventualities, including scenarios they would never wish on themselves.
(If you want access to more exclusive content and briefings on security affairs, you can sign up to Rappler+, our membership program.)
