articles.title: Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
articles.summary: Around 1,800 people were arrested after nationwide protests saw outbreaks of violence and vandalism.

blocks.text: France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris.
Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.
They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.

In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.

Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.
On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the damage, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace.
Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris.
Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."
The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor.
The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process.

The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations.
CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.

Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.

In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost."
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media.
"Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.

articles.title: Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
articles.summary: Vietnam has signed a deal with non-EU members that covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, and sustainable development, among other areas.

image.caption: Vietnam and the EFTA concluded negotiations in July, more than a decade after the free trade talks officially began in 2012Image: Hoang Thong Nhat/Vietnam News Agency/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.
The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.
Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made upNorway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).
The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.
How does the deal benefit Vietnam?

The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
Is Vietnam set to replace China as the world's factory?
Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports ​to ‌Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% ‌to be tariff-free within seven ‌years, ​the Norwegian government said in a statement.
According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.
Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.
It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

articles.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
articles.summary:
Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds

For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the…

blocks.text: For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.
Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.
Allow TikTok content?

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.
after newsletter promotion
These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.
Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

blocks.caption: The Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021.  Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.
Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

blocks.caption: The Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019.  Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

articles.title: ‘Our river is almost dead’: What’s killing an iconic Miramichi fishery?
articles.summary: As Atlantic salmon populations in the Miramichi watershed dwindle, striped bass are surging — and tensions are riding high.

image.caption: Angler Rip Cunningham, right, with guide Daniel Storey and their catch of an Atlantic salmon on the Miramichi. (Submitted by Rip Cunningham)

blocks.text: Every veteran salmon angler, guide and outfitter in the Miramichi watershed remembers their first encounter with a striped bass.
For Rip Cunningham, a member of the storied Black Brook Salmon Club, it happened at the junction of the Main Southwest Miramichi River and the Cains River.
“I caught what I thought was a salmon, and I was going, ‘This fish isn’t jumping. This is odd,’” he said. He reeled it in.
“The guides who live on the river, who’d been fishing on the river for years, said ‘What’s that?’ They had no idea whatsoever.”
It was a striped bass, a fish Cunningham believes now represents an existential threat to the Miramichi’s most iconic species: his beloved wild Atlantic salmon.
Byron Coughlan, who runs the County Haven fishing lodge near Blackville, was guiding two salmon anglers from New England about 15 years ago when they caught two bass.
“They said, ‘Your river's done,’” he recalled. “‘The bass is going to eat everything.’ They said, ‘Eventually you won’t have any salmon.’”
LISTEN | The saga of salmon, striped bass and the Miramichi:
Atlantic Voice26:10A tale of two fish on the Miramichi
The community of anglers, guides and outfitters in the Miramichi watershed fear that prediction is now on the verge of coming true.
Juvenile salmon, they say, are being gobbled up on their migratory trek to the ocean by a growing striped bass population.

“We have a crisis facing Atlantic salmon and other species on the Miramichi,” Alex Mills, an angler who is part of lawsuit against the federal government, told the House of Commons standing committee on fisheribes and oceans this month.
In 1996, the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans closed the commercial striped bass fishery to halt a collapse in stocks caused by overfishing.

The salmon anglers say the closure allowed the bass population to grow to an unsustainable level, moving upriver from its traditional home in tidal waters and throwing off the Miramichi’s delicate balance.

Bradford Burns, background, fly fishes for Atlantic salmon on the Southwest Miramichi River. Burns, an American, has been coming here from the U.S. to fish for decades. The angler in the foreground is Dawson Hovey. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
DFO blamed for ‘a big mess’
The anglers say the growth of the striped bass is killing the fabled recreational salmon fishery, once an economic lifeline for small communities along the river.
DFO officials “have done essentially nothing” to curb the bass boom “and created this big mess,” said Bradford Burns, a Maine business owner with a salmon camp on the Southwest Miramichi.
The bass population is now north of 500,000 — some estimates are much higher — while salmon returns were below 5,000 in 2025, DFO numbers indicate.

Burns, Cunningham, Mills and two other anglers have filed a lawsuit in federal court hoping to force DFO to resume a commercial bass fishery to reduce the population and give more smolts a chance to reach the ocean.

“This extraordinary level of predation is completely unsustainable and is on the verge of extirpating Atlantic salmon from what has long been considered the greatest salmon river in North America,” the group wrote in a letter to the federal fisheries minister in 2024.
Salmon are so tied to the identity of the Miramichi region, highway signs depict the fish. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

On its website, DFO says bass eat “variable numbers” of smolts every year, and “it is not clear whether this natural predator-prey dynamic is limiting the number of returning adult salmon to the Miramichi river.”
‘A direct correlation,’ outfitter says
Brock Curtis, who operates an outfitter store in Blackville that is an essential destination for anglers and guides, says the cause and effect are clear.
“Our numbers are dropping as the bass numbers are increasing, and there's a direct correlation there,” he said.

The Atlantic salmon is so tied to the river’s identity that its image is used on provincial road signs identifying the Miramichi river route. Curtis says what’s at risk is a unique fishery that puts a premium on patience, practice and a calm state of mind.
“We live in a world where a lot of people are used to immediate gratification,” he said.
“This sport isn't like that. It's a skill, and you put your time in and you will be rewarded in the end.”
Brock Curtis runs a salmon-angling outfitting store in Blackville. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
Striper success
By contrast, the abundant striped bass has spawned a two-day frenzy of immediate gratification that unfolds downriver every May.
Hundreds of anglers crowd into the city of Miramichi for the Striper Cup, a bass tournament with a seemingly bottomless list of prizes and giveaways.
"We’ve always had fish,” participant Barry Hay said in an interview over the side of his boat during this year’s tournament. "We’ve never won, but we’ve always had fish, two a day."
Dwayne Ogilvie of Salisbury said he loves the “aggressiveness” of the bass.

The Striper Cup launched in Miramichi in 2015 and has turned into one of the city’s biggest tourism draws. Paul McGraw, the city’s economic development officer, said the success of the event is “one hundred per cent” attributable to the booming bass population.
A striped bass is weighed during the Miramichi Striper Cup, an annual catch-and-release tournament for the fish. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
“We never, ever imagined that it would grow and develop the brand that we have with the Miramichi Striper Cup as quickly as we have done it,” he said.
McGraw would not comment on the debate involving salmon.
“We'd be naive to think there wasn't a controversy,” he said, “but that's not what we're into.”
At the cup's opening ceremony in May, pro angler Jeff Wilson, a co-founder of the tournament, urged participants to lobby politicians against a reopened commercial striped bass fishery.
“It’s really important that you folks talk to your politicians and protect this resource for our kids,” he said.
“It’s been here for millennia. They’re not bad. They’re good. Bass are good.”
Anglers pose with the first striped bass caught during the 2026 Miramichi Striper Cup. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
A detour for juvenile salmon
The anglers taking DFO to court estimate a commercial fishery of 300,000 to 400,000 bass would reduce the population to about 100,000 — enough, they say, to give the salmon a chance.
Ottawa approved a First Nations striped bass fishery of 50,000 in 2018 and increased the allowable catch to 175,000 six years later.
That maximum has not been reached, and anglers say letting non-Indigenous anglers catch that quota would be a good start.
In the meantime, the Atlantic Salmon Federation, the Miramichi Salmon Association and Anqotum Resource Management, a Mi’kmaw conservation agency, are doing what they can.

The Atlantic Salmon Federation, the Miramichi Salmon Federation, and Anqotum Resource Management are collecting juvenile salmon, known as smolts, in large spinning drums to be tagged, counted, and transported downriver in an effort to keep them safe from bass predation. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

In the spring, their teams descended on the northwest branch of the Miramichi at Wayerton to collect and tag salmon smolts and truck large numbers of them downriver, around and past the hungry bass population, so they could make it to the ocean.
“Concept-wise, it works,” said David Roth, an Atlantic Salmon Federation biologist who called the operation an emergency measure. "It's really just about the numbers that you can catch in total.
“It's not like we want to transport fish for decades to come. Where the population currently is, everything helps.”
Salmon angler Rip Cunningham calls it “a good experiment” but unlikely to make a dent in the problem.
“You cannot get enough of them in tanks and move them around to make any reasonable difference to this river,” he said.
DFO biologist looks for ‘larger mechanisms’
Roth and Joe Augustine, a biologist from Metepenagiag First Nation, said there’s no doubt the bass boom is the biggest cause of the salmon’s decline.
Roth said fewer than 10 per cent of migrating smolts in the Miramichi reach the ocean, compared to 80 per cent in other nearby rivers.
The difference? “It's definitely the massive population of striped bass that we do have in the Miramichi,” Augustine said.
Federal scientists say other factors can’t be discounted, because the decline is also happening in other rivers with fewer or no bass, including in Europe.

Joe Augustine, left, of Metapenagiag First Nation works with Anqotum Resource Management. David Roth, right, is a biologist with the Atlantic Salmon Federation. Both men and groups are involved with the smolt trucking project. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
“We don't say that striped bass do not eat juvenile salmon,” said Cindy Breau, a DFO biologist based in Moncton.

“What we are saying is that if we want to answer the question about why salmon are not returning to our rivers, we need to look at larger mechanisms and try to unravel the mechanisms involved with that.”
Breau suggested one reason Miramichi returns are lower may be the little tracking tags the conservationists insert in the smolts — weighing them down as they try to outrun hungry bass.
Climate change is also warming rivers beyond what cold-water salmon can tolerate and may be disrupting the food chains they rely on when they migrate to the ocean, Breau said.
But Mills said DFO’s science “flies in the face” of research done by conservation groups, providing the department a “half-baked justification for doing nothing.”
“It’s not climate-related. It’s not habitat-related. It’s striped bass-related, and if DFO does not see that, they are blind,” he told the House of Commons fisheries committee.
Katie Patles of Anqotum Resource Management tags a smolt as part of the conservation project to save some young salmon from being eaten by striped bass. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
MP says larger bass fishery an easy fix
Some anglers also point to industrial logging practices that may increase runoff into the rivers and reduce shade that blocked the sun’s heat.
Acadie-Bathurst MP Serge Cormier says some illegal net fishing may also play a role. But Cormier, an avid angler, said the striped bass clearly have “a big impact.”
Cormier is a member of the House of Commons fisheries committee, and he persuaded his colleagues to hold hearings this year on the Atlantic salmon.
“We need solutions. Enough talk,” he said.
While other factors DFO has identified are complicated to address, the MP said reducing the striped bass population with a revived commercial fishery “is the easiest piece to do right now.”

Paul McGraw, an economic development officer with the City of Miramichi, makes announcement's during the Striper Cup, a striped bass fishing tournament that's become a big tourism draw. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
Ottawa is spending $81.7 million on a 12-year Atlantic salmon strategy that includes climate-resilience measures, Indigenous partnerships and more transparent monitoring of stocks.
Federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson visited New Brunswick in August and met with the the Atlantic Salmon Federation and Miramichi Salmon Association.
"Let's understand that science is the backbone of what we do, but we also pay attention to the people who are closest to the resource,” Thompson said in an interview.
“And then if there's a disconnect, as there is in this instance, what is it that we need to do to find and strike that balance?"
'Is it our job to intervene?'
The Striper Cup has its own science championing the striped bass.
Dockside at the Striper Cup in May, a team of biologists from Acadia University ran the weigh station for the tournament.
Competitors returning to Ritchie’s Wharf watched the team rush their fish up to a table and submerge them in a tank before weighing them.
This year’s winning bass was 9.4 kilograms, or almost 21 pounds, the largest of almost 700 bass caught and released.
Salmon anglers say that abundance shows the species could withstand a regulated commercial bass fishery.
“We are not saying that we want to eradicate an entire striper population,” Augustine said.
“They're a native species, and it's important that they stay at decent levels as well, because they're meant to be here as well.”
But the Acadia team said it’s too soon after the bass’s near-collapse to take a chance.
“We should be able to long-term monitor before making big decisions,” said Leah Creaser, a Mi’kmaw biologist and Acadia researcher.
“Like, ‘that species is doing great, that one is not doing great,’ so there’s a game of picking and choosing because of a lot of social pressures.”
Leah Creaser, left, a researcher and student at Acadia University, checks striped bass during the weigh-in at the Miramichi Striper Cup. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

Trevor Avery, the Acadia professor and biostatistician who leads the team, said it’s “really hard to pit one species against another” when the ecosystem is more dynamic than a simple “smoking gun” scenario.
Creaser said the rebound and growth of the striped bass on the Miramichi may be an example of evolutionary history unfolding in real time.
“Is it our job to intervene? I’m not sure.”
A changing camp on a changing river
As the debate continues, some salmon outfitters have resigned themselves to a different Miramichi.
Wilson’s Sporting Camps, a lodge that dates back to 1855, has branched out into canoeing, tubing, corporate retreats, weddings, and, yes, even striped bass fishing.
“It's to the point now where our river is almost dead,” co-owner Karl Wilson said.
“There’s very few fish out there … and it doesn't seem like anybody's really doing anything about it.”
Everyone is “pointing the finger at one another” while waiting for Ottawa to act, Wilson said.
“In my opinion, it's almost too far gone.”

Karl Wilson, who runs Wilson's Sporting Camps, says he's seen declines on the river that have forced his business to pivot to include other outdoor sports and experiences beyond salmon angling. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)
Joe Augustine, though, remains optimistic.
His community’s long history with the Atlantic salmon runs through his great-grandfather, who could catch enough salmon in a day to feed his entire family for a summer.
Augustine said his father, as a child, “could hear the salmon run coming up the river to spawn. It would keep him up at night.”
There’s no choice but to be optimistic, he said.
“You have to believe that the salmon numbers are going to come back," he said. "Or then what are we doing this work for?”

“They’ve hit critical levels, but we've seen striped bass hit critical levels 20 to 25 years ago, and now look at them back in our river. It’s crazy, the amount — maybe, definitely, a little too much.
“But if it can be done with striped bass, why can't it be done with Atlantic salmon?”

articles.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
articles.summary: Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

image.caption: The Starlink satellite internet system has become a core component of Ukrainian defenseImage: Adam88/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

blocks.caption: There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in UkraineImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

blocks.caption: Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of dronesImage: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP

blocks.text: The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says US President Donald Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

blocks.text: TRUMP AND PUTIN. File photo shows US President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin during the G20 leaders summit in Buenos Aires, Argentina on November 30, 2018.
Marcos Brindicci/REUTERS
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says US President Donald Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

items: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia, claiming it will embolden Moscow to continue its aggression against Ukraine.

Trump's executive order, which waives key sanctions and tariffs related to Russia, is seen as undermining efforts to pressure Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, with Zelenskyy warning it could lead to increased Russian attacks.
The waiver has received mixed reactions, with some US politicians expressing concern over its implications for US-Russia relations and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON DC, USA – US President Donald Trump‘s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday, October 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”

An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night, October 16, waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US

The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelenskyy said Trump’s latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday. “This certainly does not stop the war.”
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment,” posting on X on Friday that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.

Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Saturday, she did not directly criticize Trump for waiving sanctions, but she said she would not have made that choice.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law” while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.

But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday’s executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate.”
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.

“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy.
But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday’s waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month, the Ukrainian leader predicted.

“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey … It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: For chefs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze, success is on the menu — but so is learning
articles.summary: Food entrepreneurs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze head back to the classroom, proving that even successful chefs still have more to learn

blocks.text: Bolinao, Pangasinan wakes to the sounds of water.

Before the first guest opens the door at Birdland Beach Club, the sea has already been at work all day, dragging itself up the sand and letting go over and over, the slow percussion of a shore town that has never known silence.

By the time the sun clears the treeline, the roast smell from the coffee bar is pushing its way out the open windows, warm and nutty, drifting across the lot where Joanna Ledesma’s Kopi Kubo Kollective stands on the highway: a coffee shop built on land with a rice field view, where the evening fog lifts.
Two hundred kilometers south, in a small dining room on D. Tuazon, Santa Mesa Heights in Quezon City, a different pot has been at work since morning.
At Nam Jai Thai Noodle House, khao soi is a study in contrast: soft egg-wheat noodles below, crisp ones on top, all meeting in coconut-curry broth.
The broth takes six to eight hours to prepare. Jeremaine Sze makes the curry paste from scratch, imports ingredients from Thailand, and works with local farms to source herbs and spices.
Just like in most things she does, there is no shortcut: no pressure cooker and no premade paste.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze with her staff  at Nam Jai Thai Noodle House. Contributed photo

blocks.text: Two women head these two kitchens. Ledesma owns the Birdland Beach Club and runs the Kopi Kubo Kollective in Bolinao, while Sze leads as the executive chef and owner of Nam Jai in Quezon City
The businesses are different. But the question that brought the two owners to the same culinary school was the same.
Although both have long been passionate about cooking, they always get the the question: “Are you a culinary graduate?”
Ledesma heard it while running a restaurant and coffee shop in Malaysia.
“Everybody’s telling me, ‘Are you a culinary graduate?’…I felt like there’s something missing on my side,” she recalled.
Ledesma knew how to cook and create menus, but the question left her feeling inadequate.
Working with a staff who had formal culinary training also brought the knowledge gap into focus.
For Ledesma, the hardest part was memorization — the terminologies refusing to stick to a 40-year-old brain.
She recalled hearing terms such as “mise en place” and “bouquet garni” and realizing she could not explain them, even as the head of the kitchen.

blocks.caption: Joanna Ledesma prepares meals for 50 people in her resort. Contributed photo
Joanna Ledesma meticulously prepares her pastry for a nine-course degustation. Contributed photo

blocks.text: It’s the same for Sze, who found herself having to look up certain words that her assistant, who is a culinary school graduate, would often use in the kitchen.
Both women had learned cooking by doing.
This time, both wanted the formal grounding to match what they already knew.
Before the resorts and the noodle houses, Ledesma and Sze were just two girls who had something to sell.
For Sze, learning to cook began with learning to taste. At home, her parents would ask what a dish needed: more salt, more sweetness, a better balance.
She was often asked to try the dish, identify what was missing, then add it herself. That early practice of testing and adjusting became a way of thinking about food.
Sze was eight when a move to Davao had her wanting to help earn money for tuition and personal expenses.

She made yema and polvoron, learning to craft these sweets through family and necessity. While this was her first foray into the culinary world, she attests that they aren’t really considered cooking.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze checks her food creation. Photo by: Jade Tan/Rappler

blocks.text: Years later, under the name Manila Flavorful Asian Favorites, Sze would run catering services and work on party trays and food carts from a studio condominium.
In peak periods, she cooked 40 to 80 trays a day, starting as early as 2 or 3 am.
It was a lot to prepare all on her own. Her husband would come home from work and face the pile of dishes at the sink, waiting to be washed.
The work filled the small space. Sze recalled cooking until late at night, with dishes and cookware covering the floor from 3 in the morning until 10 at night.
Ledesma’s first kitchen memories had her standing beside her parents and grandmother, watching them cook, tasting the food and being handed broth while the pots were still going.
In second grade, like Sze, she made sweets to sell to her classmates.

“When I was in Grade 2, I started making yema, I started making polvoron, I started making turon. I learned how to make money at a very young age because I love making food, also so I could sell them.”
Later on, while living independently with housemates who did not cook, she made a dish of ampalaya with eggs and shared it with them.
Her housemates would tell her that it tastes different, and their enjoyment encouraged her to keep experimenting with food.
“So there, when people eat my food, it makes me feel different and happy,” Ledesma shared.

blocks.caption: Joanna Ledesma cooks for her family. Contributed photo

blocks.text: Her love for cooking grew from family. Ledesma’s grandmother had a restaurant; her parents ran businesses, including a grocery and salon, and cooked at home.
In Bolinao, seafood, sea salt, and fermented fish are part of their local food landscape.

So early on, Ledesma built food businesses in the Philippines and Malaysia. She also traveled through Southeast Asia, taking short cooking courses and seeking local families who could teach her the food of their communities.
In Malaysia, she also put up a Kopi Kubo in Kuala Lumpur after staying there for two years.

In Bali, Indonesia, she went to a village in 2023 and asked her driver’s mother to show her how they made babi guling, which is similar to the Philippines’ lechon. She wanted to understand not only the recipe, but the traditions behind it.
But Ledesma graduated in finance from St. Louis University, shaped by a family that’s strongly into commerce.

In Makati, she sold healthy juices, then built Simone’s original snacks, fruits, vegetables, and meat dried into jerky. She worked the market for two to three years until she knew every vendor in the aisles and navigated the crate-stacked chaos.
Ledesma did it all, running two businesses in two countries, while raising two children.
Sze’s decision to open Nam Jai came while she was in her first trimester of pregnancy, tired of managing tray orders alone.
“The only thing that I craved during the pregnancy was having my own restaurant,” she joked.
Ledesma, meanwhile, shared it was her husband’s idea to put up a coffee shop on a lot they had bought along a highway, partly so he could have his coffee on long drives.
Amid their growing success, both Sze and Ledesma felt the need to go back to school.
At 40, with two kids and multiple businesses, Ledesma initially hesitated until she found the Center for Culinary Arts’ (CCA) professional weekend program, which had people around her age.
She traveled to Manila from Bolinao every week. During the finals, she lived in Manila for an entire month to fully focus.

blocks.caption: Chef Marco critiques the dishes prepared by students Joanna and Jeremaine at CCA. Photo by Jade Tan/Rappler

blocks.text: Sze had already taken introductory courses at CCA, but wanted more depth.
Her progression included signing up for Kitchen Discovery, Food and Culture Appreciation, Fundamentals of Culinary, and ProChef.
The credential question followed her there.
“Being a good cook is not enough,” Sze said. “People will still ask you, ‘Culinary graduate ka?’ San ka nag-aral? (Are you a culinary graduate? Where did you study?)”
The school experience tested Sze and Ledesma in various ways.
The pressure weighed in for Sze as she juggled culinary school and her business along with her pregnancy.
During classes, Sze kept her phone so she could check the CCTV and monitor the restaurant’s staff and customer flow.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze opens Nam Jai Thai Noodle House.Contributed photo
Jeremaine Sze and her husband pose for a maternity photo shoot during her CCA graduation. Contributed photo

blocks.text: For Ledesma, the lesson of formal technique arrived through heat. She was not used to a kitchen with many stoves running at once, or to washing and cleaning her own station, after being accustomed to directing operations and focusing on menu development and recipe research.
“Hindi ako sanay, mainit sa kitchen (I’m not used to it, it’s hot in the kitchen),” Ledesma shared.
But completing the work gives her a sense of accomplishment: “Oh, kaya ko pala (Oh, so I can actually do it).”
At Nam Jai’s kitchen, Sze’s culinary school habits became evident, from the color-coded cutting boards to sanitation practices and house rules.
Sze feels fully stepped into her role as a chef, confident enough to direct experienced staff, lead training, and instill cooking discipline.
“Yung seven to eight hours na broth [of khao soi], I don’t do shortcuts,” she said. “So, parang in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.”
(The seven to eight hours of cooking the broth of khao soi, I don’t do shortcuts. So, like in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.)

blocks.caption: Person, Chef, Clothing
CCA graduate Joanna Ledesma learns that culinary education complements food entrepreneurship. Photos from CCA

blocks.text: Ledesma’s kitchens also had school imprints: knife skills, ingredient evaluation, seafood technique — all of them also taught to staff and family, quietly correcting provincial habits, like how shrimp shouldn’t be boiled too long or else they turn rubbery.
Her signature dishes involve the fresh seafood of her beach town; her philosophy: all healthy, organic, pesticide-free, MSG-free, non-GMO cooking.
For Ledesma, one of the satisfying moments at graduation was when she could finally call herself a chef.
“Don’t hesitate,” Ledesma said. “If you have the means of doing culinary, please do it. It will improve you a lot, physically, mentally, and emotionally.” – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

articles.title: Adiong: Firm linked to Sara Duterte's husband a 'national security concern'
articles.summary: The company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, raises concerns beyond questions about unexplained assets, including potential national security…

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 4:26pm

The company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, raises concerns beyond questions about unexplained assets, including potential national security implications, House prosecution spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said on Sunday.
“This goes beyond non-disclosure or unexplained assets in her SALN. It goes to the very core of national security concerns,” Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.
Adiong made the statement after the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) confirmed that a company linked to Duterte and Carpio received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
According to a table the AMLC presented, P315.93 million came from mainland China, while P3.39 million came from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Duterte questioned the allegations, asking whether doing business with China was prohibited on national security grounds.

“So ano ba talaga? Bawal ba talaga ang negosyo with China kasi it is a national security risk? Parang nakakahiya na nga yung drug haul na papuntang Pilipinas galing Laos and Thailand, tapos eto pa tayo na nagsasabing, ‘Naku, it’s a national security risk na magnegosyo with China.’ Nagiging troublemaker of Southeast Asia tayo,” Duterte said.

(So what is it, then? Is doing business with China really prohibited because it poses a national security risk? It is already embarrassing that there is a drug shipment bound for the Philippines from Laos and Thailand, and now we are saying that doing business with China is a national security risk. We are becoming the troublemaker of Southeast Asia.)
Adiong said Philippine authorities should investigate possible money laundering activities involving funds from China.

“Ito ba ang rason kung bakit ang Bise Presidente ay sinasabi niyang troublemaker ang Pilipinas despite the fact na ang China ay continuous ang mga aggressive na mga activity diyan sa West Philippine Sea? Hindi man lang siya makapagsabi ng kanyang posisyon, na makapag-call out these illegal activities committed by China,” Adiong said.

(Is this the reason why the Vice President is calling the Philippines a troublemaker despite China’s continued aggressive activities in the West Philippine Sea? She cannot even state her position or call out China's illegal activities.)
“Ito ba ang rason kung bakit nasasabi niya ’yun? Kasi may mga kumpanya niya, as declared sa kanyang SALN, na tumatanggap ng remittances galing sa China,” he added.
(Is this the reason she is saying that? Because companies linked to her, as declared in her SALN, are receiving remittances from China.)

In a separate statement, House prosecution adviser Robert Ace Barbers said authorities should examine whether China was exploiting the Philippines’ political divisions amid Duterte’s impeachment proceedings to advance its interests.

“Is China simply pursuing its aggressive maritime agenda, or is it also taking advantage of our political divisions to weaken our resolve? These are questions our national security officials must examine,” Barbers said.
“The impeachment proceedings are an internal constitutional process. China has no business exploiting our political differences to advance its interests in our waters,” he added.
Earlier this month, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) reported that 101 Chinese vessels had been monitored across several West Philippine Sea (WPS) features in September 2026.
The figure was higher than the 56 Chinese vessels monitored in the disputed area in August.—MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: When the Cordillera danced down Session Road
articles.summary: The Festival of Festivals turns Session Road into a showcase of the region’s diverse cultural traditions

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The gongs came first, then the colors.

Then came women balancing clay pots on their heads, men carrying shields and spears, dancers in woven skirts and feathered headgear, baskets of grain, bamboo, chants, prayer movements, and stories that usually live several mountain roads apart.
On October 17, they all met on Session Road.
The 5th Cordillera Festival of Festivals brought together the region’s six provinces and two cities, turning downtown Baguio into a living picture of the Cordillera’s diversity.

blocks.caption: BELIEF. Tabuk City performers present Gabbok, a traditional Kalinga thanksgiving associated with the birth of a first child, during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals in Baguio City on October 17, 2026. The performance used chants, music, dance, and scenes of family life to express gratitude, b…

blocks.text: More than 500 performers joined the parade and cultural showcase, moving from the Melvin Jones area through Harrison Road, Magsaysay Avenue, and Session Road before gathering near Post Office Park.

Abra brought the Kawayan Festival, while Apayao presented Say-am. Benguet was represented by Kabayan’s Bindiyan, Ifugao by Gotad ad Ifugao, Kalinga by Pasil’s Tachok-Salip, Mountain Province by Lang-ay featuring Pasuk-ey, Baguio by Panagbenga, and Tabuk City by Gabbok.
It was easy to be dazzled. The more interesting part was figuring out what everyone was actually dancing about.

blocks.caption: TRADITION. fugao performers showcase Gotad ad Ifugao during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, traditional dances, agricultural symbols, and stories of ancestry, abundance, and community to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Abra’s performance highlighted bamboo craftsmanship, resilience, and the intersection of the province’s lowland and Tingguian, or Itneg, traditions.
Apayao’s Say-am was about thanksgiving, community, gongs, song, dance, and shared celebration.
Kabayan’s Bindiyan brought the pulse of the gangsa and a circle dance tied to victory, thanksgiving, and communal life.
Ifugao’s Gotad turned part of Session Road into a scene of ritual and daily life, with chants, rice, agricultural tools, baskets, woven objects, and movements tied to ancestry and abundance.
Pasil’s Tachok-Salip featured gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and movements that spoke of joy, unity, and connection to the land.
Mountain Province presented Lang-ay through Pasuk-ey, a Central Bontoc thanksgiving tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual.
Tabuk’s Gabbok celebrated the birth of a first child.
Baguio’s Panagbenga performance drew on the story of Bangan, an Ibaloy woman whose offering to Kabunian is linked to the Benguet pine.
Put all eight together and one thing becomes obvious.
Mayor Benjamin Magalong said that even people who have lived in the region for years still have plenty to learn about one another.
“We may be neighbors, but our customs, celebrations, languages, traditions, and histories are not all the same,” he said.
Baguio itself, Magalong noted, has long been shaped by people from across the region who came to the city and eventually called it home.
“So much of the region is already present here in our city,” he said. “And today, that becomes even more visible.”

blocks.caption: DANCE. Mountain Province performers present the Lang-ay Festival featuring Pasuk-ey: The Thanksgiving Summer Fest during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, prayer dances, and a Central Bontoc tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual, to Session Road.…

blocks.text: There were, naturally, phones everywhere. Session Road gave people plenty of reasons to point them.
But the Festival of Festivals was never meant to be reduced to a reel of costumes, choreography, and pretty pictures.
Department of Tourism (DOT) – Cordillera Regional Director Jovita Ganongan said the dances, garments, and traditions on display should be understood for what they are.
“Our festivals are not merely performances of our culture,” she said. “They are expressions of our identity, living stories of our ancestors, and a legacy we must carry forward.”
Ganongan also said the region’s cultural differences should not be mistaken for division.
“We may be different in our traditions and expressions of culture, but we are united through our heritage and our pride in who we are,” she said.

It is easy to turn culture into something decorative on a festival stage. But Cordillera traditions are tied to land, kinship, farming, ritual, memory, peace, conflict, survival, and belief. Strip away those meanings and what remains may still look beautiful, but it is no longer the whole story.
Baguio Representative Mauricio Domogan said the harder part comes after the applause.
“When the music subsides and the parade has passed, our responsibility to our heritage must endure,” he said.

blocks.caption: ABRA. Abra performers showcase the Abrenian Kawayan Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing bamboo traditions and the shared heritage of the province’s lowland and Tingguian or Itneg communities to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Tourism without losing the plot
The Festival of Festivals is also a tourism event, and nobody was pretending otherwise.
DOT Secretary Judilyn Quiachon said the Cordillera has a distinct place in Philippine tourism because of its mountains, rice terraces, food, crafts, and living cultural traditions.
But she said more visitors should not be the only goal.
Tourism should create opportunities for local businesses, farmers, artisans, guides, accommodation providers, and other workers while respecting Indigenous cultures and protecting the environment.
The point, she said, is for communities to “participate meaningfully in and benefit from tourism development.”

Ganongan put it more plainly during an earlier briefing. Tourism should “entertain and educate, not exploit,” create livelihoods without sacrificing identity, and welcome visitors without pushing communities to the margins of their own stories.

How do you invite people to look without turning culture into spectacle? How do you make traditions visible without reducing them to content? How do you welcome tourism without asking communities to perform a version of themselves that outsiders find easier to consume?
But for that morning, the people carrying the traditions remained in the middle of the frame.

blocks.caption: TRADITION. Kalinga performers from Pasil showcase the Tachok-Salip Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and traditions of celebration, unity, and connection to the land to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: A Cordillera too big for one photo
Women moved in measured steps beneath foliage headdresses while young men struck gongs behind them.

Rice was winnowed in the middle of Session Road. Farming tools became props but also reminders of where many of these traditions begin. Clay pots rose above dancers’ heads. Wooden bulul figures sat among grain and baskets. Men crouched low with gongs, then sprang back into movement.
Elders danced beside students. Older women carried traditions beside younger performers learning to inherit them.
Some spectators knew exactly what they were seeing. Others were encountering these practices for the first time.
The festival did not ask Abra to look like Kalinga, Ifugao to move like Benguet, or Mountain Province to tell the same story as Apayao.
Domogan summed it up in one line: “Identity does not require uniformity.”
By noon, the gongs had quieted. Performers were resting, spectators were drifting away, and Session Road was slowly becoming Session Road again.
After five years in Baguio, the Festival of Festivals will leave the city for the first time in 2027, with Kalinga set to host. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Whole streets in Paris ‘devastated’ by protests, says mayor, as France demonstrations continue – Europe live
articles.summary:
France’s worst protests in years saw buildings set ablaze across the country and record numbers of people arrested

In case you are still catching up with the news from yesterday, my…

blocks.text: Opening summary
France is recovering after its worst protests in years saw buildings attacked and set ablaze across the country.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in the demonstrations on Saturday, which began with protests from students over the cost of living.
However violent fringe groups came out in support of the students, which saw events spiralling out of control.
Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said.
Meanwhile in Limoges, central France, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.

Authorities in France are now waiting to see if protests will go into another day. The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
We will be following events in France and bringing you any reaction as it comes in.
Key events

items: 32m agoRecord numbers arrested in Paris
42m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: In case you are still catching up with the news from yesterday, my colleagues Kim Willsher and William Christou have this report.

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.

Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt.

Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
Record numbers arrested in Paris
Police in Paris arrested a “record figure” of 855 people during the protests on Saturday.
Agence France-Presse reported the number detained was the highest ever for a single event.
The figure forms part of the 1,200 arrested across France, as prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police had been hurt in clashes.
Meanwhile Deputy Mayor of Paris Lamia El Aaraje said the capital had been hit by “a level of violence that I believe we had never seen before”.
