image.caption: Carney said 'our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected' [FILE: September 13, 2026]Image: Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta.
"A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta," Carney said in a post on X.
He added that the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities.
What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected.
"We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media.
Neither Carney nor Smith provided details on the cause of the fire or whether anyone was injured.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

articles.title: B.C. municipal elections: Polls close in less than an hour as voters choose next mayors, councillors

image.caption: Signage in Vancouver on Oct. 7, the second day of advance voting. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

blocks.text: B.C. Votes: Municipal elections 2026

Voters in 161 B.C. municipalities go to the polls to elect their next mayor and council, school board and, in some cases, park board. Join hosts Lien Yeung and Stephen Quinn along with Jason D'Souza, Chris Walker and Justin McElroy for live coverage and analysis as results come in from from across the province.
The Latest

items: Millions of British Columbians are choosing their next local governments today, with voting open in municipalities across the province.
More than 3,500 candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., including municipalities and regional districts.
Heading into election day, local leaders were worried about confusion and low turnout given the provincial election takes place a week from today.
Polls close provincewide at 8 p.m. local time.

October 18Surrey candidates weigh new facilities and housing growthAkshay KulkarniSurrey mayor says $360M Vancouver Giants arena will be built on timeThe City of Surrey plans to build a 10,000-seat hockey arena that will be the new home of the WHL's Vancouver Giants. Surrey Mayor Brenda Locke defended the project, and said it would not lead to unnecessary costs for taxpayers while Giants majority owner Ron Toigo says the team will not immediately move to rename itself the Surrey Giants.Surrey's mayoral candidates have promised a range of new community and recreation facilities if elected, including a waterfront district, a conference centre and new pools.Building community infrastructure to serve Surrey's burgeoning population has been a big issue for years, with a 10,000-seat arena the latest major facility to be greenlit — even as the cost of the police transition weighs on the city's budget.The major candidates, however, have different ideas on how they'll balance housing and population growth to go along with those large projects.Locke says she will build on her work in the past, including approving more than 13,800 net new units.Annis and McCallum, meanwhile, are pushing back on the province's push for more dense housing centred around public transit. Annis says infrastructure needs to keep up with growth, while McCallum is pushing for the Crescent Beach and Ocean Park areas to be excluded from provincial housing legislation.Starchuk has promised to build more affordable homes on city land, with priority for family-sized homes.Troy Van Vliet is promising a family housing policy to include targets for two- and three-bedroom homes, while Honveer Randhawa says he would guarantee that building permits for single-family homes and renovations stamped by authorized firms are issued within five business days.

Race to watch: Locke and McCallum face off again in SurreyAkshay KulkarniWho will be the next mayor of Surrey?CBC’s The Early Edition brought together five candidates vying to be mayor of Surrey for two debates: Mike Starchuk with Imagine Surrey, Surrey city councillor Linda Annis, incumbent mayor Brenda Locke, Conservative Party of Surrey candidate Honveer Randhawa and Troy Van Vilet, a Surrey builder and business owner.Much like in Vancouver, former council allies are competing for the mayoral role in Surrey, B.C.'s second-largest city by population and one whose population growth rate led Canada for many years.Incumbent Brenda Locke of Surrey Connect was formerly a councillor under Doug McCallum, the city's mayor between 2018 and 2022 who is now running again with the Safe Surrey Coalition.The pair split in 2019 over McCallum's support for an independent Surrey Police Service (SPS), with Locke preferring to stay with the Surrey RCMP.With that issue now largely in the rearview mirror — the province having ordered the transition to the SPS — Locke and McCallum join a crowded field as they aim for the city's top job once again.Among those on the list are Coun. Linda Annis, who leads the Surrey First slate, and former MLA and councillor Mike Starchuk, leader of the Imagine Surrey slate.Two candidates — Honveer Randhawa of the Conservative Electors Association and Troy Van Vliet of Surrey Now — haven't held elected office before.

Property taxes a key issue in VancouverAkshay KulkarniVancouver Mayor Ken Sim promises tax freeze and community centres if re-electedVancouver Mayor Ken Sim made his final State of the City address for his first term to the Board of Trade on Wednesday, and with it came two big election promises. Justin McElroy reports on what the mayor is putting front and centre in his platform. Sim swept to power with a super-majority in 2022 on the back of a campaign largely focused on public safety.After four years as mayor, Sim is now promising a property tax freeze if an ABC majority is elected, after the 2026 budget featured one, too.All the other major candidates in the race have slammed that move and Sim's promise, with Fry saying the budgeted property tax freeze led to major cutbacks in city services and administration. Fry has promised more accessible, line-item budgets if he's elected.Allam has promised to cap property tax increases to the rate of inflation, while Hardwick is also promising "predictable increases" in line with inflation.Bligh has promised to replace the property tax freeze with increases based on long-term planning.

Race to watch: Vancouver mayoral race features 5 main slatesAkshay KulkarniVancouver’s mayoral field shifts into focusAfter a week where two Vancouver mayoral candidates left the race, voters are getting a clearer sense of the main choices on the ballot next month. As the CBC's Justin McElroy reports, they’re all trying to position themselves in slightly different ways.The leaders of five major political slates are aiming to be mayor of B.C.'s most populous city.They include the incumbent, Ken Sim of ABC Vancouver, and his former chief of staff, Kareem Allam, who is running for the Vancouver Liberals.Two longtime councillors — Pete Fry of the Vancouver Greens, and Rebecca Bligh of Vote Vancouver — are also in the race, as is former councillor Colleen Hardwick of TEAM Vancouver.Bligh was kicked out of ABC Vancouver last year while Hardwick ran for council in 2018 with Sim, who was then the NPA's mayoral candidate.Fry was the only opposition voice in the previous council for a period of time due to councillor vacancies and an ABC super-majority.

What does a local government do?Arden McLeodWhat municipalities can and can’t do in B.C.With municipal and provincial elections going on at the same time, it can be hard to know which promises being made at the local level are realistic, and which ones aren’t. The CBC’s Justin McElroy explains what powers cities actually have.Many major funding and policy decisions sit with the province and its ministries. But Kimberly Speers, who teaches public administration at UVic, says people can feel the impact of local government decisions every day."It's not generally seen as, you know, an exciting part of governing ... but at the same time, my gosh, are those local services so, so important," Speers said.Municipalities like Vancouver tend to spend the most on protective services, such as police, fire, and emergency services.Another big ticket item for municipalities is utilities like water, sewage and waste. Municipalities also oversee parks, recreation and culture centres and how land-use is determined — as well as maintaining sidewalks, roads and public transportation.

Multiple votes to cast in civic electionsArden McLeodElection overload is real in B.C. ahead of 2 back-to-back votesElection overload is real in B.C. with 2 back-to-back votesMunicipal political parties generally don't map neatly onto provincial parties across B.C., and depending on where you live, polling can include elections for bodies like school boards, as well as for mayor and council.In Vancouver, for instance, residents are voting for one mayor, 10 city councillors, seven park board commissioners and nine school board trustees.In provincial elections, on the other hand, voters simply choose one candidate to represent their riding in the legislature.

Record number of advance voters in some municipalitiesAkshay KulkarniA cyclist heading toward an advance voting station in Vancouver. (Nav Rahi/CBC)Vancouver is among many municipalities that saw a record number of residents make use of advance voting opportunities for this election.The city says 103,000 voters cast a ballot over four advance voting days, smashing a record of 65,127 in 2022. Officials also say mail-in voting requests doubled compared to 2022, with 21,000 requests this year.Surrey and Kelowna, among others, also saw high advance voter turnouts.Every municipality was required to provide at least one advance voting day in B.C.That's encouraging because, despite a local government's major impact on voters' lives — given they are usually responsible for day-to-day services like garbage collection, sewage and policing — voter turnout in B.C.'s civic elections are usually lower than provincial and federal elections.In 2022, 29.2 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot, well below the turnout for the subsequent provincial and federal elections, according to CivicInfoBC.

(Nav Rahi/CBC)British Columbians are choosing their next local representatives on councils, school boards and other regional posts on Saturday, the first of two election days this month.The Union of B.C. Municipalities says more than 3,500 local government candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., which include municipalities and regional districts. CBC's Decision Desk will be closely following the vote count after polls close across most of the province at 8 p.m. local time, and will deliver projections of the results in some of B.C.'s biggest communities, including Kamloops, Kelowna, Richmond, Surrey, Vancouver and Victoria.The overlapping provincial election had many worried about widespread voter confusion. Still, many cities and municipalities reported increased or even record turnout at advance polls, including Vancouver, Richmond, Burnaby, Kamloops, Surrey, Kelowna, Prince George, Cranbrook and View Royal.Voters will cast their ballots again next Saturday for the provincial election.

articles.title: Sara Duterte can file charges vs witnesses in impeachment trial, says law professor
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte can file charges against the witnesses in her trial following the withdrawal of three articles of impeachment against her, a law professor said on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 8:53am
Vice President Sara Duterte can file charges against the witnesses in her trial following the withdrawal of three articles of impeachment against her, a law professor said on Sunday.

"Kung gusto ng Bise Presidente na i-vindicate ang kanyang sarili, maghain siya ng karampatang kaso sa mga tumestigo laban sa kanya, ito man perjury or violation ng confidentiality," said Adonis Gabriel of San Beda University College of Law in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(If the Vice President wants to vindicate herself, she should file the appropriate charges against those who testified against her, whether it is perjury or violation of confidentiality.)
The Senate impeachment court earlier accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte.

The prosecution said that it will no longer pursue three other charges against Duterte, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business.
The Vice President can also charge the senator-judges if she wishes to, said Gabriel.
"Pwede maghain ng administrative case sa Senado mismo para tignan kung mayroong paglabag sa karapatan ng depensa ang mga huwes," he added.
(An administrative case can be filed right in the Senate to check if the judges violated the rights of the defense.)

Following the withdrawal of the three articles against her, Duterte's camp said the prosecution's withdrawal of three articles of impeachment on Tuesday is an admission that the allegations hurled against her lacked basis from the start.
"The withdrawal is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning," said lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: 'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections
articles.summary: Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control…

image.caption: It was the fourth 'No Kings' protest since President Trump returned to officeImage: Madison Swart/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters gathered across the United States for the latest "No Kings" demonstrations as Americans begin casting ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," Saturday's event aimed to fire up Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, rather than protest against President Donald Trump and his administration.

"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.
Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

blocks.caption: There were more than 3,000 'No Kings' events planned across the USImage: Daniel Heuer/REUTERS

blocks.text: Trump opposes mail-in voting

Trump repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought to restrict the practice ahead of the midterms. He regularly votes by mail-in ballot, arguing that his job makes him an exception to his criticism of the practice.
The US president blamed election fraud, without providing evidence, for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election against Democrat Joe Biden.
Various surveys have concluded that restricting mail-in ballots could benefit Republicans, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.
Opponents fear that the Trump administration may try to interfere with the midterm results, particularly if Republicans lose the majority.
Opinion polls suggest Democrats are poised to regain control of the House ​of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.

articles.title: Ebike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beaches trails
articles.summary:
Sydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54

An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged…

blocks.text: An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.

New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October.
“Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm yesterday,” police said on Sunday.

The teenager was taken to Manly police station and charged with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner in or near a public place, and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent.
On Saturday, police had released CCTV images of a male they believed could assist with inquiries.
Police allege that 11 separate incidents occurred against girls and women aged between 13 and 54.
The investigation was initially launched after three separate alleged incidents on 7 and 8 October.

“In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an ebike,” police said on Saturday. In one of the incidents, the offender allegedly made “inappropriate sexual comments”.
At Narrabeen lagoon about 4.30pm on 1 October the suspect “allegedly sexually touched [a] woman before riding away on an ebike,” police said.

Last Monday, police received a further report that between 5pm and 5.30pm that day, two women walking along the Narrabeen lagoon near Bilarong reserve had been sexually touched by a male riding an ebike.
Strike Force Mexvo was established to investigate the incidents with assistance from state crime command’s sex crimes quad.
Speaking in Narrabeen before Saturday’s arrest, Supt John Duncan urged members of the public to come forward with any information about the alleged incidents.
“It’s a bushland park that runs 8km, a large amount of which … runs through bushland, obviously there’s not a great deal of CCTV and cameras.”
The 13-year-old was granted conditional bail to appear at children’s court on 4 November.

articles.title: Arizona joins Nevada to fight proposed cuts to their shares of Colorado River
articles.summary:
Move comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water supplies

Arizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to…

blocks.text: Arizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to their shares of the shrinking Colorado River.

The move comes after the interior department announced restrictions this summer that could slash the water supplied to lower basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – over the next two years depending on the river’s condition.
The river’s major reservoirs, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have plummeted to historically low levels, due to overuse and a changing climate.

The states sharing the waterway were at an impasse with the upper basin states arguing that their downstream counterparts were responsible for the reservoir’s water shortages and should thus face the largest cuts.
The federal government’s intervention came after the states missed several deadlines for a consensus.
The fear looming over the state of the river is that if reservoir levels plunged far enough, the waterway would effectively not be able to flow downstream, a so-called deadpool.
The upper basin states – Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico – were spared from the water cuts, an exemption that has drawn sharp rebuke from the leaders of the lower basin states.
“We are drawing a line in the sand,” Arizona governor Katie Hobbs said in a Friday statement.

“I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona, and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement,” Hobbs continued, referring to a two-year-voluntary water conservation pact among her state, California and Nevada.

Tom Buschatzke, the director of Arizona’s water department, said “intervention in the Nevada lawsuit is necessary at this time for Arizona to protect its legal rights to Colorado River water while preserving a path forward to achieving a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada to protect the Colorado River system”.
An interior department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the joint litigation.

articles.title: Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after lung cancer surgery, as his surgeon said there are "no clinical reasons" to prevent his planned trip to Latin America next month.

image.caption: Pope Leo leaves a hospital in Rome on Saturday. (Gregorio Borgia/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after lung cancer surgery, as his surgeon said there are "no clinical reasons" to prevent his planned trip to Latin America next month.
Surgeon says pontiff should be fit for upcoming Latin American tour
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."
Leo, 71, is scheduled to make an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
"As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," Margaritora said.

Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, well ahead of the weeklong hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
Pope says he feels 'much better'
"I am much better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV.
Leo greeted patients inside the hospital accompanied by his surgeon, before waving to well-wishers outside who cried out "Holiness" as he walked to a waiting vehicle.

items: Pope back on his feet, eating normally following cancer diagnosis

blocks.text: He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter's Square last December — an encounter she told reporters "gave her the strength to overcome the illness."

Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.

He will take on his first official duty on Sunday, delivering the traditional Angelus blessing to the faithful in St. Peter's Square. It comes exactly one week after the pontiff revealed to throngs in the square that the nodule had been found and would be surgically removed — an unusually candid revelation for the Vatican.
Further tests being carried out

Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital, also confirmed that the nodule was discovered by chance during routine abdominal examinations. It appeared as "a small spot" at the base of the lung, which extends down to the diaphragm, he said.
He added that if the spot had been higher up, "it certainly would not have been seen."
The cancer was in its early stages, and the pope had "no respiratory symptoms, and felt perfectly well," Margaritora said.
Pope Leo urges compassion for migrants during Spain trip

He described Tuesday's procedure to remove the lobe as "routine" and "without complications," but acknowledged that it "stirred deep feelings ... to operate on a pope, who for the first time — at least in modern history — is undergoing surgery for a malignant tumour."

The Vatican did not disclose that the tumour was malignant until after Tuesday's successful surgery. It later confirmed that the pope had undergone a biopsy before being admitted to Gemelli. Experts say the state-of-the-art Ion robotic bronchoscopy would have indicated whether the tumour was malignant and possibly whether cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.

items: AI's 'paradise of machines' a threat to humanity, Pope Leo says

blocks.text: Histological testing of the tumour and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumour's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumour's genetic characteristics.
Margaritora said the pope's recovery so far had required "very little assistance from us."
"His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect. It was truly commendable," the surgeon said.

articles.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
articles.summary: Satellite images give clues about how Kim spends his holidays - something far out of reach for most North Koreans.

blocks.text: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
Image source, Vantor/BBC
BySoram CheonBBC Korean and Aghnia AdzkiaEast Asia Visual Journalism
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.
What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.
After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.
This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.
It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

blocks.caption: A satellite image showing an 80-metre-long vessel from above, with waterslides on the left side and a large, four-lane swimming pool measuring around 50 metres in length.

blocks.text: "In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho.
Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.
The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures.
The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.

blocks.caption: A graphic showing satellite images of vessels docked at the Wonsan maintenance dock in a 2×2 grid. The images are dated, clockwise from the top left, 24 October 2025, 31 January 2026, 9 July 2026 and 12 April 2026. The October 2025 image shows vessels measuring approximately 55m and 80m long. The…

blocks.text: Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.
But the regime has long been known to live in luxury.

We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.

While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.

blocks.caption: A close-up satellite image of the Wonsan area, with locator points marking Wonsan Villa, Wonsan Maintenance Dock, Kalma Peninsula, Tae Island and Sin Island.

blocks.text: Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.

A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.

North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.
North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.

State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.

blocks.caption: Image caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma

A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.
For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.
Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.
Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".

Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living
The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.
The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.

blocks.caption: Two satellite images dated 4 July 2026 and 9 October 2026, showing an 80-metre-long vessel off the Kalma Peninsula.

blocks.text: Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.

blocks.caption: A satellite image dated 25 Aug 2026 shows two vessels, the 50m and 55m, off Tae and Sin Islands close to Wonsan.

blocks.text: Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.

blocks.text: Image source, Vantor
The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.

Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".
The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.

blocks.caption: A satellite image taken on 9 July 2026 showing a 60-metre-long vessel anchored off Wonsan Villa, alongside a close-up of the vessel.

blocks.text: Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.

blocks.caption: A satellite image taken in November 2002 showing an 80-metre-long vessel anchored off Wonsan.

blocks.text: Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.
He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.

To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first.
"Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."
Graphics by: Arvin Supriyadi

articles.title: How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
articles.summary: Demonstrations across the country turned violent, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked.

blocks.text: An estimated 550,000 people took part in protests across France, demanding greater investment in education and action on the rising cost of living.
The demonstrations quickly descended into violence, with cars and buildings set alight and shops ransacked.
At least 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday as riot police deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
The unrest follows weeks of student-led protests, with demonstrators joining forces to express growing anger over economic conditions and French President Emmanuel Macron handling of the crisis.
In a social media post, Macron denounced the violence and said that vandals and looters will be "prosecuted and punished".
BBC correspondent Adina Campbell reports from Paris.

articles.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
articles.summary: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.

blocks.text: Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on Saturday
ByNick Thorpe
CorrespondentReporting fromTirana, Albania
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.

George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday

blocks.text: Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital

blocks.text: Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".

He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.

Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

articles.title: At least 17 dead in crush at Hindu festival event in India
articles.summary: Many more have been injured at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark a Hindu festival.

blocks.text: At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.
The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.
Six of the dead have been identified, Adhikari said.

A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.".
Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions.
Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump
articles.summary: Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why…

image.caption: Ilhan Omar has been the subject of repeated attacks by Donald TrumpImage: Richard Tsong-Taatarii/Star Tribune/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?
Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

blocks.caption: Minneapolis, the capital of Minnesota, is home to the largest Somali community in the United StatesImage: Jessie Wardarski/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.
Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

blocks.caption: Officers from the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.
'Timing wildly suspicious' — Unpacking the search of Ilhan Omar's home
Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic Party's candidate to represent the state of Michigan in the US SenateImage: Emily Elconin/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Plover, not a fighter: masked lapwing nesting on Tasmanian cricket ground indifferent as play continues
articles.summary:
While masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good innings

At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside…

blocks.text: At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside Launceston in northern Tasmania, a masked lapwing has claimed prime real estate in the middle of a community sports ground, showing complete indifference to the weekend cricket matches taking place around it.
Warming a nest of eggs, the bird has been affectionately dubbed “Faf Swoop Plessis” by locals – a play on former South African cricket captain Faf du Plessis.
Because the species is protected under state law, carrying fines of up to $21,300 for disturbing nests, ground staff have had to mow around the site, while players steer clear.
During a match early in the season, Great Northern Raiders player Caleb Brewer drew the short straw and was stationed directly beside the nest.
“At the start it was pretty weird, but towards the middle we kind of got used to it and the plover wasn’t too bad at the end,” Brewer told local paper The Examiner.
The following weekend, Riverside first-grade opener Josh Partridge was tasked with fielding near the plover, but reached a peaceful “mutual understanding”, according to The Examiner.

“It was like the plover knew there was a game of cricket going on,” he said. “We weren’t interfering with what was going on in its life, so it didn’t want to interfere with what was going on in ours.”
That kind of sporting truce is common, according to Mark Holdsworth OAM from BirdLife Tasmania.

“Lapwings will often become accustomed to the local patterns of people using a site and in many situations people modify their behaviour to avoid the core nesting area,” Holdsworth said. Everyone has learned to live with each other.”

While masked lapwings – widely known across Australia as plovers – have an intimidating call and reputation for swooping during spring nesting season, choosing a wide-open lawn is actually a calculated survival tactic.
Sports ovals are a “fantastic place” for them to nest, Holdsworth said, because unobstructed views mean parent birds can spot threats early.
Sean Dooley from BirdLife Australia also said that what looks like eccentric behaviour to humans makes sense for plovers.

“The places they choose to nest can seem crazy from our perspective, but there is logic to it,” Dooley said. “They like to nest out in the open so they can see danger coming and they rely on camouflage to hide their eggs and their chicks. So by nesting on an oval, they have a clear view in all directions.”
He said that when people give the bird a wide berth, lapwings generally realise they are not under threat.
“They definitely aren’t out to get us by nature, they really only care about making sure their chicks aren’t being threatened …

“Swooping isn’t their only tactic; they also put on a display that mimics having a broken wing to lure potential threats away. They’re just being good parents and doing all they can to protect their young.”

Lapwing eggs hatch after 28 to 30 days of shared incubation by both parents. If a clutch is infertile, incubation can continue for several weeks, while birds will often nest again at the same site if their eggs are destroyed.
after newsletter promotion
Once hatched, the chicks quickly leave the nest. Dooley said parent birds carry stray egg fragments away to avoid attracting predators, before guiding their offspring across the turf.
“If we can just give them their space, they can move away from the nest area once they are walking,” he said.
The West Tamar mayor, Christina Holmdahl, said council maintenance teams look after dozens of parks and sporting grounds across the municipality, encountering at least 10 nesting sites every year.

“Given the protected listing of the masked lapwings in Tasmania, our staff take their responsibility of looking after these birds very seriously and take extra precautions to protect the birds and any nests they find,” Holmdahl said.
Council workers maintain strict buffer zones around the birds and their nests when conducting maintenance.
“The plovers never act aggressively towards our staff on the ground,” she said.
The standoff coincides with the annual Aussie Bird Count which runs from Monday 19 October.

Now in its 13th year, the national citizen science project invites the public to record bird sightings to help researchers track how native species are coping with urban development and a changing climate. Last year, the Australian magpie was the most commonly spotted species, while the rainbow lorikeet recorded the highest overall tally.

“The count is a great opportunity to discover the birds that share your neighbourhood and understand more about them,” BirdLife Australia’s James Johnson said.” For many of us, that’s likely to include the amazing masked lapwing.”
Register for the 2026 count here.

articles.title: Almost all NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of flammable vegetation
articles.summary: Exclusive: Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Climate and environment correspondent

blocks.text: Almost every home destroyed in New South Wales during the black summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found.

The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep homes safe.
The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season.
More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals.
Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research, published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire, found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees.

The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps of bushfire prone land that firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be.

Associate professor Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”.
“That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said.
But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost.
When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the Forest Fire Danger Index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” said Price.
“That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.”

He said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas, including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses.
Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia.
“Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said.
The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost.
after newsletter promotion

Melissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”.
“The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well.
“This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.”
O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area.
Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed to remove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres.
She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk.
“We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as well as extreme pyroconvective fires,” she said.
Inspector James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast.
“They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said.
“We could be in for a challenging fire season.”

articles.title: Ontario to import U.S. electricity this winter, months after Ford threatened to cut power exports
articles.summary: Ontario will import power from the United States this winter, the province's independent electricity operator has announced, just a few months after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut exports to the…

blocks.text: Toronto

Ontario will import power from the United States this winter, the province's independent electricity operator has announced, just a few months after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut exports to the U.S. amid the ongoing trade war.
Province's electricity operator signs 6-month contract with U.S.-based Alpha Generation
Ontario set to import New York electricity this winter after Ford threatened to cut the U.S. off

The contract will help secure additional short-term capacity for the winter, while "facility maintenance" takes place, the Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) said in an Oct. 1 news release about the deal.
The six month contract with U.S. based Alpha Generation for 600 megawatts will start on Nov. 1, IESO said.
While IESO did not detail the maintenance work taking place, the province began a multi-year refurbishment project at the Pickering Nuclear Generating Station in September.
The contract undercuts recent statements by the Ford government, according to Lewis Krashinsky, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University who studies U.S.-Canada politics.

IESO is an independent body that monitors the province's electric grid and is not associated with the provincial government. Despite that, Krashinsky said the contract will "undercut" Ford's position on using electricity as a bargaining chip with the U.S.
Ontario is exporting seven time more electricity to neighbouring jurisdictions than it did in 2025, said the IESO in an emailed statement. (Colin Butler/CBC)
"For all the tough talk, I think it doesn't look at all that good for Doug Ford," he said.

In August, Ford said he was willing to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the U.S. as the trade war drags on. Ontario sends power to about 1.5 million people in Michigan, New York and Minnesota.
"The best [Ford] can hope for is that this story doesn't hit too many American outlets," Krashinsky said.
"[If it reaches] the ears of senior American leaders, they're going to just say, 'Great, we're cancelling this contract or we're not taking you seriously, because you still need our energy too.'"
Contract part of 'normal' planning: IESO

Despite the new contract, Ontario is a "net-exporter of power," IESO said in an emailed statement Friday. IESO's mandate is to ensure a reliable and affordable supply of electricity for Ontarians, it said.
Ontario is exporting seven times more electricity to neighbouring jurisdictions, such as Quebec and New York, than it imported in 2025, IESO said.

The Alpha Generation contract is a part of "normal system planning" to secure additional short-term capacity as a way to manage "system-wide maintenance needs" and to cover peak demand over the winter months, IESO said.
CBC News asked Alpha Generation for more information on the deal.
The province did not respond Friday to questions on the contract, referring CBC News to IESO.
This Pickering, Ont., nuclear plant is getting a revamp
Province needs to invest in clean energy: expert

Keith Brooks, programs director for advocacy group Environmental Defence Canada, argues the province could have avoided importing electricity from the U.S. entirely by shifting to more clean energy sources in the past few years.
The Ford government cancelled several clean energy projects and removed the requirement to create a long-term energy plan when they first came into power, Brooks said.

"The government has mismanaged this file," he said, adding the province has become overly reliant on nuclear and gas systems that are expensive to maintain and have remained active "much longer than originally intended."
"The reality is we've been burning more and more gas in Ontario because we haven't been building clean energy," he added.

In the summer of 2025, the Ford government announced the province's first-ever integrated energy plan, which seeks to secure energy for "generations to come," according to a news release from June 12, 2025. The plan includes a commitment to nuclear energy, with the goal of reaching 99 per cent zero-emissions electricity by 2050.

items: Ford doubles down on 'kiss my ass' comment to Trump amid Canada-U.S. trade war
Ford doubles down on threat to cut off energy to U.S. amid spectre of trade war

blocks.text: Ford's threats on withholding energy are "idle," Brooks said, given the U.S. provides most of the gas Ontario uses for power.
"[The U.S.] could have shut off the gas, which meant we couldn't even turn our own lights on, let alone sell electricity to them," he said.
The solution is to invest more in clean energy, including wind and solar, Brooks said. Homegrown clean energy wins "hands down" for Brooks.
"We don't need to rely upon the U.S. to give us the gas nor the electricity. We can generate it here ourselves," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Arrthy Thayaparan is a writer at CBC Toronto with interests in health, climate, education and community stories. You can contact her at arrthy.thayaparan@cbc.ca.
With files from Gabriela Silva Ponte and Lorenda Reddekopp

articles.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
articles.summary: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.

blocks.text: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.

"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."

Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.

But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".

A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."

It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".

Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.
